text: In the Posterior Analytics, Aristotle faces the threat that if all scientific knowledge (episteme) requires demonstration, then justification is either circular or regresses without end. What is his solution?
choices: Circular demonstration is acceptable, since P and Q can be mutually supporting, so no undemonstrated starting points are required.
The first principles of a science are grasped immediately and non-demonstratively by nous, halting the regress without circularity.
The regress is harmless because an actual infinity of prior premises can in fact be traversed in thought.
All scientific premises are ultimately provisional hypotheses, accepted only insofar as their observable consequences are borne out.
explanation: Aristotle's foundationalism stops the regress by holding that first principles (definitions, axioms, postulates) are known directly by nous rather than by demonstration, giving knowledge a non-inferential base. Option 3 describes the later hypothetico-deductive model that displaced Aristotle's demonstrative ideal, not his own view, and he explicitly rejects the circular route in option 0.
